li.p:
The Huntington-Hill method uses the geometric mean,
c(L,U) = \sqrt{LU},
which generalizes for more than two numbers as
c(a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_n) = \sqrt[n]{a_1 a_2 \cdots a_n}.
What if we modify Huntington Hill to use
c(L_s,Q_s,U_s) = \sqrt[3]{L_sQ_sU_s}
where Q_s is the quota for State s from the standard divisor? Try on the coffee data set.

There are two other means we could try, too. The Harmonic Mean is given by
h(L_s,U_s)= \dfrac{2 L_s U_s}{L_s + U_s},
and the Quadratic Mean is given by
p(L_s,U_s) = \sqrt{\dfrac{L_s^2+U_s^2}{2}}.
Apply these to the coffee data.
Describe how to generalize each of these to more than two numbers.

subsubsection.title: Formal Mathematical Variables
subsubsection.p: The problem can be defined using the following parameters:

dl.dd: A positive integer representing the total number of items to be distributed (for example, the total number of seats in a legislative body).
The number of entities receiving the items (for example, states or political parties).
An n-dimensional real vector representing the size of each entity (such as population or vote counts).
The sum of all entries in \mathbf{a}, given by A = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i.
An integer vector where m_j is the final number of units allocated to entity j, satisfying \sum_{j=1}^n m_j = M and m_j \ge 0.

subsubsection.title: The Exact Quota
subsubsection.p: A central concept in apportionment is the exact quota, denoted q_j, which represents the ideal fractional share of units an entity would receive if units were divisible. It is defined by

In an ideal mathematical world, we would have m_j = q_j. However, because m_j must be an integer and q_j is typically a real number, an apportionment method is required to map the real vector of quotas to an integer vector of allocations.

subsubsection.title: Mathematical Constraints and Properties
subsubsection.p: For an apportionment method to be considered fair or valid, it is often expected to satisfy certain mathematical axioms:

ul.li: Symmetry. The outcome should not depend on the order in which the entities are listed.
Homogeneity. If all input values a_j are multiplied by the same positive constant, the resulting apportionment should remain unchanged.
The Quota Rule. A method satisfies this rule if each allocation m_j is either \lfloor q_j \rfloor or \lceil q_j \rceil.
House Monotonicity. If the total number of units increases from M to M+1, no entity’s allocation m_j should decrease. This property rules out paradoxes such as the Alabama Paradox.

subsubsection.title: Error Minimization
subsubsection.p: From a mathematical perspective, many apportionment methods can be viewed as attempting to minimize the error between the ideal proportions q_j and the actual integer allocations m_j. This is often modeled using a decomposable error function

where \varphi_j measures the severity of the error for entity j. For example, the Sainte‑Laguë method can be characterized as minimizing an error function based on the squared difference between allocated units and exact quotas.

subsection.title: Apportionment Polyhedra
subsection.p: An apportionment polyhedron is a geometric region within the space of all possible exact quota vectors \mathbf{q} that a particular apportionment method maps to a single, fixed integer seat allocation \mathbf{m}. In mathematical terms, it consists of all fractional quota vectors that result in the same whole-number distribution of seats.

subsubsection.title: Geometric Representation
subsubsection.p: The concept is best understood by visualizing the space of exact quotas.

ul.li: The set Q. This set contains all possible fractional distributions of M items among n entities. For example, if there are three parties and M = 5 seats, the set Q forms an equilateral triangle in three-dimensional space with vertices at (5,0,0), (0,5,0), and (0,0,5).
Integer points. Within this geometric space, the possible integer seat allocations are represented by discrete lattice points corresponding to integer vectors \mathbf{m}.

Defining the polyhedra. A valid apportionment method partitions the larger region Q into smaller regions, or polyhedra, each associated with a single integer allocation. Any exact quota vector lying inside a given polyhedron is rounded or mapped to the integer allocation corresponding to that region.

subsubsection.title: Function and Boundaries
subsubsection.p: The shape and size of apportionment polyhedra depend on the error function or rounding rule associated with the chosen apportionment method.

ul.li: Mapping. A desirable property of an apportionment method is that any exact quota vector that is already an integer vector is mapped to itself.

Borders. The boundaries between apportionment polyhedra correspond to tie situations, where an exact quota vector may be equally compatible with two or more integer seat allocations. In such cases, the method must include a rule for resolving ties along these boundaries.

subsection.title: Using Apportionment Polyhedra to Assess Fairness
subsection.p: The apportionment polyhedron provides a geometric framework for assessing the fairness of an apportionment method by describing how the method rounds exact quotas—the ideal fractional shares of seats—into whole-number allocations. By analyzing the shapes and boundaries of these polyhedra, mathematicians and social scientists can determine which methods minimize rounding error and which are susceptible to representational paradoxes.

subsubsection.title: Visualizing Rounding and Error
subsubsection.p: Geometrically, the space of all possible exact quota vectors Q is partitioned into regions, or polyhedra, each associated with a single integer seat allocation.

ul.li: Mapping fairness. A well-behaved apportionment method maps any exact quota vector lying inside a given polyhedron to the integer allocation at its center. Fairness can then be assessed by measuring the gravity of the error, defined as the distance or discrepancy between the ideal quota q_j and the resulting integer allocation m_j.

Defining boundaries. The boundaries between polyhedra correspond to tie situations, in which an exact quota vector may be equally compatible with more than one integer allocation. A fair method must resolve such ties using a consistent rule, rather than an arbitrary choice.

subsubsection.title: Comparing Methodological Justness
subsubsection.p: Different apportionment methods correspond to different error functions, and these choices lead to distinct polyhedral decompositions of the quota space. This geometric perspective allows for direct mathematical comparison between methods.

ul.li: Sainte‑Laguë versus Hare. Different methods induce different polyhedral grids. The Sainte‑Laguë method is designed to minimize relative error and, in three-entity settings, produces a hexagonal tiling that is often regarded as neutral with respect to entity size. In contrast, rounding methods such as Hare’s method focus on greatest remainders and are frequently analyzed using \ell_p-norms—such as Euclidean distance—to identify the integer point closest to a given exact quota.

Bias detection. Geometric analysis can reveal systematic biases in an apportionment method. For example, linear divisor methods may favor smaller entities or larger entities depending on the placement of their polyhedral boundaries, often parametrized by an initial divisor offset.

subsubsection.title: Identifying Paradoxes
subsubsection.p: Apportionment polyhedra are also a useful tool for determining whether a method satisfies common axioms of fairness.

ul.li: The Quota Rule. Polyhedral analysis can be used to check whether allocations always lie between the floor and ceiling of the exact quotas.

House monotonicity. Examining how polyhedral boundaries change as the total number of seats M increases helps determine whether a method avoids decreases in allocation when additional seats are added.

The Alabama Paradox. Poorly aligned polyhedral boundaries can lead to paradoxical outcomes in which increasing the total number of seats causes an entity to lose a seat, a phenomenon observed in historical legislative apportionments.

subsubsection.p: A contemporary illustration of these issues arose in the 2020 Iowa Democratic caucuses. The use of Hamilton’s method, which satisfies the Quota Rule but is geometrically vulnerable to paradoxes, produced several aggregation anomalies in which the sum of local allocations failed to align with statewide totals.
